summary.text: A Rust session core connects terminal, protocol and SDK clients to a model–tool loop.

maturity.text: Public history reaches back to April 2025. Stable releases coexist with active alpha development.

advantages.text: Explicit boundaries between clients, turn execution and operating-system sandboxing.
A long public history makes architectural changes unusually traceable in this comparison.

tradeoffs.text: The large Rust implementation and multiple client protocols create a demanding first code-reading exercise.
The open repository does not represent every part of the hosted product ecosystem.

taskFit.text: Local repository work where execution policy and OS containment are important.
Headless automation and applications built on the app-server protocol.

nodes.label: Session / TurnContext
nodes.subtitle: Shared Rust core

responsibility.text: Owns a turn, its context and the repeated sampling cycle. A tool request leads to another model sample after the result is returned.

nodes.inputs: Prompt, session state and steering input
nodes.outputs: Model requests and durable turn events
nodes.extension: Clients enter through the CLI or the app-server protocol.
nodes.failureMode: Cancellation and compaction failures must preserve input for a recoverable turn.

nodes.label: Model request
nodes.subtitle: Context → next action

responsibility.text: Samples the configured model with conversation context and available tools.

nodes.extension: Model configuration changes the provider-facing request.
nodes.failureMode: A failed or cancelled request cannot be treated as a completed response.

nodes.label: Tool router
nodes.subtitle: Resolve a tool call

responsibility.text: Runs requested tools and supplies their output to the next sample. Tool execution remains separate from model sampling.

nodes.outputs: Tool output associated with its call
nodes.extension: Native tools and MCP extend the set of callable operations.
nodes.failureMode: A tool error becomes part of the continuing conversation.

nodes.label: Rollout + state
nodes.subtitle: Durable conversation

responsibility.text: Persists thread activity so clients can resume and inspect work across turns.

nodes.extension: The app-server protocol exposes thread operations.
nodes.failureMode: Stored conversation state does not undo an external tool's effects.

nodes.label: Skills · hooks · MCP
nodes.subtitle: Context and tool seams

responsibility.text: Adds reusable instructions, lifecycle interception and external tool connectivity around the core loop.

nodes.outputs: Additional context, tools or hook decisions
nodes.extension: Skill files, hooks, plugins and MCP servers.
nodes.failureMode: An extension's presence does not mean it is loaded or trusted in every session.

nodes.label: Approval policy
nodes.subtitle: Allow · ask · deny

responsibility.text: Decides whether a requested action may run under configured policy. Human approval and OS restrictions serve different purposes.

nodes.extension: Managed configuration and lifecycle hooks participate in policy.
nodes.failureMode: Approval alone does not constrain a process after it starts.

nodes.label: OS sandbox
nodes.subtitle: Process · files · network

responsibility.text: Constrains execution using platform backends. The Linux design uses filesystem and namespace boundaries around the command.

nodes.inputs: An authorized command and execution policy
nodes.extension: The containment mechanism depends on the operating system and selected mode.
nodes.failureMode: A more permissive execution mode changes the boundary; do not assume all commands are equally contained.

chapters.title: The turn loop
chapters.heading: Inside a coding turn
chapters.body: Follow a request from the first prompt to a tool result.
chapters.takeaway: The model proposes actions; the harness controls the loop that executes them.

chapters.title: Tools and approval
chapters.heading: Before a tool runs
chapters.body: Follow the proposed action through routing and policy. The permission decision is distinct from the execution boundary.
chapters.takeaway: A tool call is a request, not an unconditional command.

chapters.title: Execution boundary
chapters.heading: Where a command can act
chapters.body: Inspect the OS sandbox and compare it with the approval policy above it.
chapters.takeaway: Approval answers whether. Containment limits where and how.

chapters.title: Session memory
chapters.heading: What survives a turn
chapters.body: The shared core records conversation activity for continued work and protocol clients.
chapters.takeaway: Persistence supports resumption; it is not a rollback of the outside world.

chapters.title: Extensions
chapters.heading: What can be added
chapters.body: Skills, hooks, plugins and MCP add instructions, interception and capabilities around the Rust core.
chapters.takeaway: A new capability need not replace the entire turn loop.
